what_its_for: This medicine helps your body make more white blood cells after chemotherapy. Chemotherapy can lower your white blood cell count, which makes it easier to get serious infections. This medicine lowers your chance of getting those infections by boosting your immune system.
how_to_take: This medicine comes as a shot given under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in your stomach area, upper arm, or thigh. A healthcare provider may give it to you, or you or a caregiver may be taught how to give it at home using a prefilled syringe. Always follow your doctor or nurse's instructions on exactly how to inject it. Do not shake the syringe. Let it warm to room temperature for about 30 minutes before injecting. Do not use it if it looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles in it.
dosing: The usual adult dose is one injection (6 mg) given once per chemotherapy cycle. It is typically given at least 24 hours after your chemotherapy is finished. Do not give this medicine within 14 days before your next chemotherapy treatment. Your doctor will decide the exact timing that is right for you.
missed_dose: This medicine is usually given just once per chemotherapy cycle. If you miss your scheduled injection or forget to give it, contact your doctor or nurse right away. Do not try to guess when to give an extra dose on your own.
storage: Keep this medicine in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do not freeze it — if it accidentally freezes, thaw it in the refrigerator once. If it freezes a second time, throw it away. You may store it at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for no more than 3 days. Throw away any medicine kept at room temperature for longer than 3 days. Keep it out of reach of children. Dispose of used syringes safely in a puncture-resistant sharps container.
what_to_avoid: Do not receive this medicine within 14 days before or 24 hours after chemotherapy. Avoid shaking the prefilled syringe. Do not use if the liquid looks unusual. Tell your doctor before starting if you have sickle cell disease, as this medicine may trigger a sickle cell crisis. Avoid donating blood or bone marrow while using this medicine without talking to your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you notice: severe pain in your upper left stomach area or left shoulder (this could be a sign of a spleen problem); sudden or severe breathing trouble, fever, or chest pain; swelling of the face, lips, or throat (signs of an allergic reaction); very sore bones or muscles that does not go away; unusual tiredness, pale skin, or dark urine (possible signs of a serious blood condition called capillary leak syndrome); pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site that gets worse. Also call your doctor if you develop a fever or any signs of infection.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working within 1 to 2 days after your injection, but the full benefit — a rise in your white blood cell count — is usually seen within 3 to 4 days. White blood cell levels typically return to normal about 2 weeks after the injection. Your doctor may check your blood counts to see how well it is working.
special_populations: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as the safety of this medicine during pregnancy and breastfeeding is not fully known. If you have sickle cell disease, use this medicine with caution as it may cause a sickle cell crisis. This medicine has not been fully studied in children, so ask your doctor before using it in a child. Older adults can generally use this medicine, but should be monitored closely for any side effects.
